Brain Health
and Longevity

Brain mapping (qEEG) gives an objective, measurable picture of how your brain is functioning, read alongside your hormonal and metabolic health.

Book an appointment Neurological health →
Clinically reviewed by Dr Gina Schoeman · Harley Street & Wimbledon · CQC registered
Overview Symptoms Why missed Diagnosis Treatment Why us Questions Book
Overview

What Is Brain Mapping (qEEG)?

Most tests of brain function look for damage or disease: a scan for structural change, a standard EEG for seizure activity. They rarely look at how the brain is actually functioning day to day, the patterns behind attention, stress recovery, sleep, emotional regulation and learning that don't show up as "abnormal" on a conventional test but still shape how someone thinks, feels and copes, at any age.

Brain mapping (quantitative EEG, or qEEG) is a non-invasive assessment that records the brain's electrical activity and compares it against a normative reference database for the patient's age, revealing which regions and networks are working harder than they should, and which are underactive. It doesn't replace a neurological or developmental work-up. It adds a layer conventional testing doesn't cover: an objective, measurable picture of brain function itself, from childhood attention and learning patterns through to adult stress, cognitive performance and long-term brain health.

At The Schoeman Clinic, brain mapping is led by Simona Turlică, our neuro-regulation and brain mapping specialist, and read alongside the hormonal and metabolic picture the clinic already builds for every adult patient. Across every age group, cognitive, attentional and emotional symptoms are rarely a brain-only problem. In adults they are frequently connected to hormonal shifts, particularly through perimenopause and andropause, and to metabolic and stress-system patterns that a standalone brain mapping provider has no way of seeing. For patients already managing a diagnosed neurological, psychiatric or developmental condition, brain mapping and the training that follows sit alongside their existing specialist's care. They support how someone is functioning day to day and are never a replacement for it.

Symptoms

Symptoms Brain Mapping Can Help Explain

01

Brain mapping is relevant across a wide range of ages and presentations, wherever attention, learning, emotional regulation or cognitive performance has changed, or hasn't developed as expected, in ways that are hard to pin down on a standard assessment.

02

Children and adolescents. Attention and concentration difficulties, learning difficulties, behaviour that raises questions around autism spectrum presentations, developmental delays, and adolescent anxiety or difficulty regulating emotions.

03

Attention, executive function and performance. Distractibility, difficulty sustaining focus, disorganisation and impulsivity, including presentations of ADHD in adults that were missed in childhood, particularly common in women whose symptoms don't match the hyperactive-boy stereotype most clinicians are trained to recognise. This also covers CEOs, senior professionals and athletes wanting to sharpen focus, decision-making and recovery under sustained pressure, with no clinical presentation at all.

04

Emotional regulation and mental health. Chronic overwhelm and burnout, low mood and depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive patterns, trauma-related stress and PTSD, and panic attacks, where a patient wants an objective picture of what's happening alongside their existing mental health care.

05

Cognitive change and neurological conditions. Mild cognitive impairment, and the cognitive and attentional changes that can accompany neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, and Alzheimer's or another dementia, in patients who are already under a neurologist's care.

06

Everyday cognitive and sleep symptoms. Brain fog, memory lapses, disrupted or unrefreshing sleep, and mood swings that don't track cleanly with anything else going on.

07

For many adult women, cognitive and attention symptoms cluster around perimenopause and are misattributed to stress or ageing alone. For men, the equivalent andropause-linked pattern is even less often recognised, simply because there's less vocabulary for it. In both cases, a hormonal driver and a measurable change in brain activity are often part of the same picture.

Why missed

Why Changes in Brain Function Are So Often Missed

Standard neurological and mental health assessment is built to detect specific, defined problems: structural damage on a scan, seizure activity on a standard EEG, a diagnosable mood disorder against a symptom checklist, a behavioural checklist for developmental concerns. Functional change, a brain working differently rather than visibly abnormally, sits outside what most of those tools are designed to catch with any precision.

In children, developmental and attentional concerns are often assessed through observation and parent-reported questionnaires alone, without an objective physiological measure to sit alongside the behavioural picture. In adults, and particularly in women, ADHD and other attention-regulation differences are frequently missed altogether in childhood and only surface, or worsen, during a major hormonal transition like perimenopause, by which point they're usually attributed to stress, anxiety or "just getting older" rather than investigated as a distinct, measurable pattern.

A ten-minute GP appointment built around "how are you feeling" or "how is he doing at school" doesn't have the tools to turn a subjective description into an objective finding. The result is a familiar pattern across every age group: normal-looking test results, a label of "just stress" or "just a phase," and the actual, measurable pattern behind the symptoms left unexamined.

For patients already managing a mental health diagnosis or a progressive neurological condition, the gap is different but just as real. Specialist appointments are typically built around symptom review and medication management, with little room to track how brain function itself is changing session to session. Similarly, high performers under sustained pressure rarely have their brain function assessed at all, because nothing about how they're coping looks clinically "wrong."

Diagnosis

How We Assess Brain Function With a qEEG Brain Map

Brain mapping starts with a qEEG recording: a comfortable cap with sensors that read the brain's electrical activity while the patient sits at rest, eyes open and closed, adapted for age and, in children, kept short and low-stimulation. That raw data is compared against an age-matched normative database, producing a map of which regions and frequency bands are overactive, underactive, or poorly coordinated relative to expected patterns for that age group.

Simona Turlică interprets the map in clinical context, not as a standalone printout. Findings are considered alongside the five areas below. That combination, brain activity read alongside the rest of the patient's physiology and history, is what distinguishes this from a standalone brain mapping service.

  1. 01

    Hormonal markers

    Particularly relevant in adults, where cognitive, attention or mood symptoms may be linked to perimenopausal, andropausal or other hormonal change.

  2. 02

    Metabolic and thyroid markers

    Both known contributors to cognitive fog and fatigue in adults.

  3. 03

    Developmental and behavioural history

    In children and adolescents, alongside input from parents, teachers or other clinicians already involved.

  4. 04

    Symptoms and lifestyle context

    Reported symptoms, including sleep, stress load and occupational or academic demands.

  5. 05

    Existing diagnoses and specialist care

    Where a patient is already under a neurologist, psychiatrist or other specialist for a diagnosed condition, so the map is read as part of that wider picture rather than in isolation.

Treatment

Our Approach: Neurofeedback and Brain Training

Brain mapping identifies a pattern. Treatment is about training the brain toward better regulation, using the map as its starting point and its benchmark for progress, with the approach tailored to the individual's age and presentation.

Brain mapping and neurofeedback are wellness, cognitive and developmental training tools designed to support how the brain is functioning day to day, not to treat, cure or claim to slow the progression of a named condition. This distinction matters most for patients managing a diagnosed mental health condition, such as depression, anxiety, OCD, PTSD or panic attacks, or a neurodegenerative condition, such as Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, or Alzheimer's or another dementia: for these patients, brain mapping and neurofeedback are used alongside their psychiatrist's, neurologist's or GP's ongoing care, never in place of it, and no outcome or improvement is guaranteed. Where a map or a consultation raises something that needs fuller investigation, or a level of risk (such as an indication of active crisis or a finding suggestive of a seizure disorder), the patient, or their parent or guardian, is referred on to the appropriate specialist immediately.

  1. 01

    Neurofeedback

    Real-time training that helps the brain learn to shift out of the patterns identified on the map, building better self-regulation over repeated sessions. Used with both adults and children, with protocols adjusted for age and attention span.

  2. 02

    Photobiomodulation (PBM)

    Targeted light-based support, calibrated to the individual's brain map, used alongside neurofeedback where appropriate.

  3. 03

    Hormonal and metabolic correction

    In adults, where the map and the wider work-up point to a hormonal or metabolic contributor, that is addressed directly rather than treated as a separate issue.

  4. 04

    Developmental and behavioural support

    For children and adolescents, findings are used to inform practical strategies for attention, learning and emotional regulation, coordinated with parents, schools and any other specialists already involved in the child's care.

  5. 05

    Performance training

    For executives, other high-performing professionals and athletes, the same assessment and neurofeedback approach is used to support focus, decision-making and recovery under sustained pressure, distinct from any clinical presentation.

  6. 06

    Re-mapping

    Follow-up qEEG assessment to track change against the original baseline and adjust the protocol accordingly.

Why us

Why Choose The Schoeman Clinic for Brain Mapping (qEEG)?

Brain mapping at The Schoeman Clinic is delivered by Simona Turlică, trained across qEEG, neurofeedback, biofeedback and photobiomodulation, and a member of the International Society for Neuroregulation and Research (ISNR). Her approach is built on objective, measurable data rather than a subjective impression of how someone says they're feeling, or how a child is presenting at school.

What makes it distinctive here is the same principle behind every discipline at the clinic: nothing is read in isolation. In adults, a brain map is interpreted alongside hormonal and metabolic results; in children and adolescents, it's interpreted alongside developmental and behavioural history; for patients already under specialist care for a mental health or neurological condition, it's interpreted alongside that care, in coordination with their existing team. Either way, it's read by a clinical team working to one methodology, delivered through a service that holds full CQC registration, with a clear referral pathway to paediatric, psychiatric or neurological specialists wherever a finding needs it.
